newsitem.title: USA: U.S. SPR oil sale "off the table," Pena says.
newsitem.headline: U.S. SPR oil sale "off the table," Pena says.

text.p: U.S Energy Secretary Federico Pena said Friday a proposed sale of $1.145 billion of crude oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve in 2002 was "off the table."

Speaking to reporters after addressing the Independent Petroleum Association of America, Pena said the five-year balanced budget deal between the White House and Congress did not contain the oil sale.

The White House's budget plan had called for the sale in 2002 as a way to reduce the deficit, but Pena had said he felt the proposal was just a budget "placemarker" and said he would try to find ways to avoid it.
Energy Department senior adviser Kyle Simpson said removing the sale had "been in the mill for a few days, and we finally worked it out."
In the ongoing budget debate, Pena said, "We're going to work bery hard to keep it off the table."
Pena said halting the sale "will send a very strong message" to other members of the International Energy Agency "that we are very serious about energy security."
The IEA had raised concerns about the planned sale, saying it was risky to cut the reserve as U.S. oil imports and oil use were rising.
IEA officials also said it sent the wrong signal to other countries that the agency said needed to pay more heed to their energy security.
"We hope that the leadership we're showing will be reflected in the work with other countries," Pena said.
The budget agreement counts on revenue from leasing excess capacity in the SPR to other countries, but the budget plan counted on that raising a fairly nominal amount of revenue, Simpson said.

Pena also said he preferred a one-year extension of the Energy Policy Act, which oversees the SPR, because he is afraid Congress would not be interested in ideas to change the way the reserve is managed if the extension were longer.
The Energy Department plans to offer legislation later this year which Pena has said would more accurately reflect the way the reserve is managed now.
Senate Energy Chairman Frank Murkowski, an Alaska Republican, is pushing a five-year reauthorization of the act, saying there could be risky lapses of the law with a one-year extension.
"We're concerned that there is a potential of losing interest in Congress in looking at the more comprehensive" changes in the SPR program if the law gets long-term reauthorization, Pena said.
